newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan March industrial output.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan March industrial output.

text.p: Japan's industrial output in March fell a preliminary 1.5 percent from the previous month on a seasonally adjusted basis, the Trade Ministry said on Monday.
The ministry also forecast manufacturers' output would rise 1.9 percent in April and rise 1.1 percent in May.
Following are economists' comments on the data.
KOJI SHIMAMOTO, INDUSTRIAL BANK OF JAPAN

"Forecasts for April and May are both positive but this is exaggerated by technical factors such as holidays in May. It also seems that there is some car production still coming through in May. But there will be some reaction from a rise in the sales tax (on April 1), and June could be quite a large fall."

"We're seeing a much stronger recovery in output than many people anticipated. It's going to be harder and harder to deny the strength in the economy. We are seeing strong output figures, we are seeing strong employment figures, we are seeing strong import figures -- all of which points to a recovery in domestic demand."

"Certainly the strong forecasts for both April and May are very encouraging. Forecast revisions in the industrial production series are a very reliable indicator of the status of the business cycle and we are continuing to see upward revisions. This suggests that sentiment is improving among manufacturers."

"In February there was a huge drop, and the same in March, a minus growth rate. So the basic trend of the Japanese industrial production is not such a strong one. The near future outlook for Japanese industrial production is not such a strong one because there are many uncertain matters such as the consumption tax hike and the stop to tax cuts."

"That production plans for April and May are both positive reinforces the impression that production is quite firm. Capital spending, capital goods and exports are all firm and pushing production up."

"Though May's figures are affected by the holidays, if you take away this factor, then the May figure would be almost flat. Also worth noting is the fact that inventories are down significantly, 2.6 percent (in March), which bodes well for future production."
